source: Faraday's Law with Calculus
ε = −dΦ/dt for loops that rotate, grow or sit in changing fields.
Students use an average ΔΦ/Δt over a long time when asked for the emf at one instant.

You know Faraday's law as "a changing flux makes an emf", with Lenz's law giving the direction. With flux as a function of time and the derivative, we can find the emf at any instant, not just an average over an interval.

$$\role[emf]{voltage}{\varepsilon} = -\role[number of turns]{constant}{N}\frac{\role[tiny change in magnetic flux]{field}{d\Phi_B}}{\role[tiny time interval]{time}{dt}}.$$ The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current makes a field that opposes the change. For $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, the product and chain rules give one term for each thing that changes.

Faraday found that the emf depends on how fast the flux changes, not on how big it is. "How fast, at this instant" is a derivative. Dividing a change by a time interval, $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$, only gives the average emf over that interval; letting the interval shrink to zero gives the emf at one moment. The sign is fixed by energy: if the induced current reinforced the change, it would feed itself without limit.
A coil in a field that ramps up, holds steady, then ramps down. The emf graph follows the slope of the flux graph: zero while the flux is steady, however large it is.
Worked examples
A 50-turn coil of area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$ sits in a perpendicular field $B = 0.020t^2 + 0.10t$ (tesla, seconds). Find the emf at $t = 2.0\ \text{s}$.
A field that speeds up
$|\varepsilon| = 0.0900\ \text{V}$
$\dfrac{dB}{dt} = 0.040t + 0.10$, which is $0.18\ \text{T/s}$ at $t = 2.0\ \text{s}$.
A circular loop in a steady $0.50\ \text{T}$ field (perpendicular to it) grows: its radius is $10\ \text{cm}$ and increasing at $2.0\ \text{cm/s}$. Find the emf.
A growing loop
$|\varepsilon| \approx 6.28\ \text{mV}$
$\Phi = B\pi r^2$, so $\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = B\cdot 2\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt}$ by the chain rule.
A field through a loop rises from $0$ to $0.50\ \text{T}$ in $10\ \text{s}$, all of it in the last second. Compare the average emf with the emf during that last second.
Average or instant?
zero, then ten times the average
The average over all $10\ \text{s}$ uses $\Delta\Phi/(10\ \text{s})$.
For the first $9\ \text{s}$ nothing changes, so the emf is zero. In the last second the flux changes ten times faster than the average rate, so the emf is ten times the average.

Using an average $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$ over a long time when the question asks for the emf at one instant. Unless the flux changes at a steady rate, the average hides what happens at any particular moment. Write $\Phi(t)$, differentiate it, and put in the time you want. Check: if $\Phi(t)$ is not a straight line in time, the emf cannot be constant.
